_**The Texas Chainsaw Massacre**_ is a 2003 American [slasher film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slasher_film "Slasher film") serving as a [remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_remake "Film remake") of [Tobe Hooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobe_Hooper "Tobe Hooper")'s 1974 film _[The Texas Chain Saw Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Texas\_Chain\_Saw\_Massacre "The Texas Chain Saw Massacre")_, and the fifth installment in [_The Texas Chainsaw Massacre_ franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(franchise) "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (franchise)"). It was directed by [Marcus Nispel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Nispel "Marcus Nispel") (in his feature directorial debut), written by [Scott Kosar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Kosar "Scott Kosar"), and produced by [Michael Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bay "Michael Bay") and [Mike Fleiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Fleiss "Mike Fleiss"). The film's [ensemble cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast") includes [Jessica Biel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Biel "Jessica Biel"), [Jonathan Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Tucker "Jonathan Tucker"), [Erica Leerhsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erica_Leerhsen "Erica Leerhsen"), [Mike Vogel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Vogel "Mike Vogel"), [Eric Balfour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Balfour "Eric Balfour"), and [R. Lee Ermey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Lee_Ermey "R. Lee Ermey").

Like its source material, the plot follows a group of young adults traveling through rural [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") who encounter [Leatherface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherface "Leatherface") and his murderous family. Several crew members of the original film were involved with the project: Hooper and writer [Kim Henkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Henkel "Kim Henkel") served as co-producers, [Daniel Pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Pearl_(cinematographer) "Daniel Pearl (cinematographer)") returned as cinematographer, and [John Larroquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Larroquette "John Larroquette") reprised his voice narration for the opening [intertitles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertitle "Intertitle").

The film was released in the United States on October 17, 2003, received mixed reviews from critics and was a commercial success. It grossed $107 million at the box office on a budget of $9.5 million. A [prequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prequel "Prequel") was released in 2006, subtitled _[The Beginning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Texas\_Chainsaw\_Massacre:\_The\_Beginning "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning")_. _The Texas Chainsaw Massacre_ was the first film to be produced by [Platinum Dunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_Dunes "Platinum Dunes"), who would go on to produce remakes of several other 20th-century horror films.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

On August 18, 1973, five young adults – [Erin Hardesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Hardesty "Sally Hardesty"), her boyfriend Kemper, her brother Morgan, and their friends Andy and Pepper – are traveling to a concert after visiting [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") to purchase [marijuana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marijuana "Marijuana"). While driving through [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), they pick up a traumatized hitchhiker walking in the middle of the road. She tells them they're going the wrong way and forces Kemper to stop the van. Speaking incoherently about "a bad man", she commits suicide with a revolver hidden in her dress.

The group finds a gas station hoping to contact the police. The store's proprietor, Luda Mae, tells them to meet [Sheriff Hoyt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheriff_Hoyt "Sheriff Hoyt") at the Old Crawford Mill. Instead, they find [Jedidiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_characters#Jedidiah_Hewitt "List of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre characters"), a young boy who says Hoyt is at home [getting drunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binge_drinking "Binge drinking"). Erin and Kemper go through the woods to find his house, leaving Morgan, Andy, and Pepper at the mill with Jedidiah. They come across a plantation house, and Erin is allowed inside by [Monty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_characters#Monty_Hewitt "List of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre characters"), an amputee, to call for help. Kemper goes inside to look for Erin, and is hit in the head with a sledgehammer by "[Leatherface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherface "Leatherface")", who drags him into the basement.

Meanwhile, Hoyt arrives at the mill and takes possession of the hitchhiker's body. After Erin discovers that Kemper is missing, she and Andy return to Monty's house. There, Erin distracts Monty, while Andy searches for Kemper. After realizing that Andy is inside, Monty summons Leatherface from the basement with his cane and he attacks Andy with a chainsaw. Andy fends him off as Erin escapes. After a brief chase Leatherface catches up to Andy and saws off his left leg. Carrying Andy to the basement, Leatherface impales him on a meat hook. Erin returns to the mill, but before she and the others can leave, Hoyt arrives. He reassures them everything will be fine but when he finds marijuana on the dashboard, Hoyt then orders the three of them to get out of the van and get on the ground, and instructs Morgan to reenact the hitchhiker's suicide using her gun. Morgan attempts to shoot Hoyt, but the gun is unloaded. Hoyt handcuffs Morgan and drives him back to the house, beating him along the way and also taking the van's key with him.

Erin and Pepper manage to hot-wire the van but the wheels fall off. They are attacked by Leatherface, now wearing Kemper's face as a mask. While attempting to run, Pepper is killed by Leatherface. Erin runs and hides in a nearby trailer belonging to the "Tea Lady", an obese middle-aged woman, and Henrietta, a younger woman who gives her tea that has been drugged. Erin discovers that they have kidnapped the hitchhiker's baby, but passes out before she can escape. Erin wakes up at the house, surrounded by the Hewitt family: Leatherface, his mother Luda Mae, Hoyt, Monty, and Jedidiah.

In the basement, Erin finds Andy still hanging on the meat hook. When she can't lift him off the hook, Erin uses a knife to put him out of his misery. She then finds a wounded Morgan handcuffed in a bathtub and the two flee the basement as Leatherface gives chase. Jedidiah, who disagrees with his family's actions and who was forced by Luda Mae to stay out with their dogs, leads them out of the house and distracts Leatherface while they escape. Erin and Morgan find an abandoned shack in the woods, and barricade themselves inside. Leatherface breaks in and discovers Erin. Morgan attacks Leatherface, who hangs him from a chandelier by his handcuffs and kills him with the chainsaw. Erin escapes into the woods with Leatherface in pursuit. The chase continues into a slaughterhouse, where Erin attacks Leatherface with a meat cleaver and severs his right arm.

Erin runs outside and flags down a trucker, whom she tries to convince to drive away from the house the same way the hitchhiker did, but he stops to find help at the gas station. She sees Luda Mae & Hoyt talk to the trucker while Henrietta watches the baby. As Henrietta walks outside to give Luda Mae her raincoat, Erin sneaks the baby out of the eatery, and places her in Hoyt's car. She hot-wires the car and Hoyt tries to stop her, but she runs him over repeatedly until he is dead. Leatherface then appears in the road and slashes the car with his chainsaw, but Erin escapes with the baby. Two days later, two officers investigating the house are killed by Leatherface, and the case remains open.

In November 1998, it was reported Unapix Entertainment has acquired theatrical rights to _[The Texas Chainsaw Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Texas\_Chainsaw\_Massacre\_(franchise) "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (franchise)")_ and had begun pre-production on a fifth installment tentatively titled _TX25_ for a 1999 release.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-UnapixChainsawVar-5) However, by January 2002 Unapix Entertainment had allowed their option on the rights to expire.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-RadarVar-6)

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Development")]

On December 5, 2001, Creature Corner.com reported that [Michael Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bay "Michael Bay")'s newly created company [Platinum Dunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_Dunes "Platinum Dunes") (which was created in order to produce low-budget films), had set its focus on remaking _[The Texas Chain Saw Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Texas\_Chain\_Saw\_Massacre "The Texas Chain Saw Massacre")_. Early announcements on the site indicated that the story would be told in flashback with actress [Marilyn Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Burns "Marilyn Burns"), who starred in the original film, reprising her role as an aged [Sally Hardesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Hardesty "Sally Hardesty") recounting the events in the film. It was later announced that the filmmakers had already purchased the rights to the original film.

Early in the film's production the original filmmakers [Tobe Hooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobe_Hooper "Tobe Hooper") and [Kim Henkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Henkel "Kim Henkel") would be writing a script for the film, but it was unknown at the time whether or not their script would be used. In June 2002, it was announced that [Marcus Nispel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Nispel "Marcus Nispel") would direct the film in his directorial debut.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-Mania.com-7) Nispel said that he was initially against the idea of remaking the film, calling it "blasphemy" to his longtime director of photography, [Daniel Pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Pearl_(cinematographer) "Daniel Pearl (cinematographer)"), who had shot the original film. Pearl, however, encouraged Nispel to join the project, as he wanted to bookend his career with _Chainsaw_ films.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-8)

It was later announced that [Scott Kosar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Kosar "Scott Kosar") signed on as the film's screenwriter.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-9) As in the original 1974 version, it is loosely inspired by the real-life crimes of [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin") serial killer [Ed Gein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Gein "Ed Gein"). Gein's crimes had also inspired novels such as _[Psycho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho\_(novel) "Psycho (novel)")_ and _[The Silence of the Lambs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Silence\_of\_the\_Lambs\_(novel) "The Silence of the Lambs (novel)")_, both of which were later adapted into subsequent films.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-10)

### Screenplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Screenplay")]

The screenplay was written by Scott Kosar, who went on to write the screenplays for _[The Machinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Machinist "The Machinist")_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-11) and Platinum Dunes' [remake of _The Amityville Horror_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Amityville_Horror_(2005_film) "The Amityville Horror (2005 film)").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-kosarinterview-12) The film was Kosar's first professional job as a screenwriter and later recalled feeling both thrilled and honored at the prospect of writing the screenplay for the remake. Kosar also realized early on that he was dealing with "one of the seminal works of the genre" and one that could not be bettered. When discussing with the film's producers, Kosar felt that the new film shouldn't try to compete with the original film, as he felt that it was made under different circumstances.

In earlier drafts Erin, the film's main character, was revealed to be nine months pregnant throughout the film but was removed from later drafts at producer Michael Bay's insistence.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-nispelinterview-13)

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Casting")]

[Jessica Biel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Biel "Jessica Biel"), who previously starred in the television series _[7th Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th\_Heaven\_(TV\_series) "7th Heaven (TV series)")_, was cast as the main character Erin.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-Mania.com-7)

Actor [Andrew Bryniarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Bryniarski "Andrew Bryniarski"), who starred in Bay's _[Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl\_Harbor\_(film) "Pearl Harbor (film)")_ and stayed friends with him afterwards, personally met with producer Bay and asked him for the role of Leatherface. Another actor, named Brett Wagner, was cast for the role before Bryniarski, but, on the first day, the actor was hospitalized and fired for lying about his physical abilities. Without an actor for the film's main antagonist, the filmmakers called and asked if Bryniarski still wanted the role, which he accepted. To prepare for the role, Bryniarski ate a diet of brisket and white bread in order to get his weight to nearly 300 pounds. Bryniarski would later reprise his role as Leatherface in the film's [prequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre:_The_Beginning "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-Interview_with_Andrew_Bryniarski-14)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Filming")]

Nispel favored shooting the film in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), but Bay suggested [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), where he had previously shot three times.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-ign-bay-15)[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began in [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas") in July 2002[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-16) and lasted 40 days.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-ign-bay-15) Nispel intentionally shot the film in a different style, using more traditionally narrative elements, as he did not want to make a shot-for-shot remake replicating the original film's documentary-like style.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-17) Cinematographer Pearl explained from an on-set interview: "People ask me, 'Is it going to be as gritty and grainy as the last one I did?' No. I did that. There's no point in making the exact same film with the exact same look."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-18)

The remake includes references to the previous film, including [John Larroquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Larroquette "John Larroquette"), who returns in his role as the film's narrator.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEElliott-Smith2016181-19)

The weather during filming was very hot and humid. Bryniarski, who portrays Leatherface in the film, did all his own stunts and was forced to wear a "fat suit", which increased his near-300 lbs to 420 lbs. The suit also heated up quickly, so the actor had to ensure that he drank a lot of fluids before a shoot. Leatherface's mask was also a problem; the mask was made out of [silicone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone "Silicone") and was difficult for the actor to breathe through. The crew had many prop chainsaws for actor Bryniarski to use, such as chainsaws that put out smoke, and live chainsaws.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-Interview_with_Andrew_Bryniarski-14)

## Reception

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Box office")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/EricaLeerhsenChainsawPremiere.jpg/250px-EricaLeerhsenChainsawPremiere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EricaLeerhsenChainsawPremiere.jpg)

The film grossed $10,620,000 on its opening day and concluded its opening weekend with $29.1 million in revenue, debuting at number 1 at the U.S. box office.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-odessa-24) Within 17 days of its release, the film had grossed over $66 million in the US.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-32)

The film opened in various other countries in the following months (including a Halloween release in the United Kingdom)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-bbc-33) and grossed $26.5 million, while the North American gross stands at $80.6 million, bringing the worldwide gross to $107 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-BMojo-3) The film's budget was $9.5 million, making it the highest-grossing film of the franchise even when adjusted for inflation. Adjusted for inflation as of 2018 the film would have grossed over $162 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-BMojo-3)

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Critical response")]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 37% of 155 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 4.9/10.The website's consensus reads: "An unnecessary remake that's more gory and less scary than the original."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-34)[Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 38 out of 100, based on 33 critics, indicating "generally unfavorable" reviews.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-Metacritic-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-36) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "B+" on an A+ to F scale.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-CinemaScore-37)

[Manohla Dargis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manohla_Dargis "Manohla Dargis") of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ praised the polish of Pearl's cinematography (in contrast to his grittier work in the original), though noted: "The remake moves faster and sounds louder, but comes off as callous rather than creepy."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-38) Robert K. Elder of the _[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")_ gave it three out of four stars and called it "an effectively scary slasher film" despite its absurd premise.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-39) William Thomas of _[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire\_(film\_magazine) "Empire (film magazine)")_ rated it three stars out of five and wrote: "You'll have to overcome resentment towards this unnecessary remake before you can be properly terrorised but, on its own terms, it plays well."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-40)[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") gave the film a rare zero stars out of four, calling it "A contemptible film: Vile, ugly and brutal. There is not a shred of reason to see it. Those who defend it will have to dance through mental hoops of their own devising, defining its meanness and despair as 'style' or 'vision' or 'a commentary on our world'."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-41)_[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ gave the film an unfavorable review, writing that the film was an "initially promising, but quickly disappointing retread of a hugely influential horror classic".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-42)

[Peter Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Travers "Peter Travers") of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ awarded the film two stars out of four, writing: "Director Marcus Nispel, acclaimed for his ads and music videos, has a sharp eye and the good sense to hire Daniel Pearl, who shot the first _Chainsaw_. But all the bad-rehash mojo from _[Friday the 13th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday\_the\_13th\_(1980\_film) "Friday the 13th (1980 film)")_ to _[The Blair Witch Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blair\_Witch\_Project "The Blair Witch Project")_ has infected Scott Kosar's script. Hooper went for primitive, Nispel goes for slick. Hooper went easy on the gore, Nispel pours it on" and called the film "soulless".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-43)[Dave Kehr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Kehr "Dave Kehr") from _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ gave the film an unfavorable review, noting: "Rather than exhilaration, this bilious film offers only entrapment and despair," further commenting that the film was about as much fun as sitting in on an autopsy.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-44)[Leonard Maltin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Maltin "Leonard Maltin") awarded the film 1.5 stars out of four, complimenting the film's intensity but criticized the lack of likable characters and the lack of humor which was present in the original, stating, "Once it kicks into gear, it's brutally unrelenting toward its unappealing characters and the audience."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaltin20131397-45)

On [SBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_(Australian_TV_channel) "SBS (Australian TV channel)")' _[The Movie Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Movie\_Show "The Movie Show")_, Australian critic [Margaret Pomeranz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Pomeranz "Margaret Pomeranz") said this was the first film she has walked out of (giving it half an hour) and declined it a rating while fellow host [David Statton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Stratton "David Stratton") rated it one star.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-46) "I was in a cinema and there was about 10 single men sitting around, and I just thought, I don't have to see this", she says. "So yes, I did walk out. I choose to embrace movies, but there is a lot of average movies out there. You just have to try and look at the good things in them. Certain genres are not to my taste — prison dramas, man's cruelty to other men or women … I used to embrace violence in cinema in a lot of ways, but I'm reacting against that."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-47)

The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s Jamie Russell gave the film some praise, referring to it as "a gory, stylish, and occasionally scary push-button factory of shocks and shrieks remarkably better than anyone had the right to expect." but goes on to lament, "if the filmmakers could churn out something this decent, why didn't they shoot an original script, or even a sequel to Hooper's 1974 classic instead of a remake?"[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-bbc-33)_[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_'s [Peter Bradshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bradshaw "Peter Bradshaw") awarded the film two stars out of five, referring to it as a "bullish revival" of the original, adding: "The movie finds tastily grotesque [Diane Arbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Arbus "Diane Arbus") locals to freak out our poor heroes and heroines. Everything is as unsubtle as you like, and let's face it, unsubtlety is the order of the day."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-48)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Due to the film's financial success, it influenced a plethora of horror movie franchises to remake their original films across the span of the 2000s and 2010s. Notable examples include _[House of Wax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_of\_Wax\_(2005\_film) "House of Wax (2005 film)")_, _[The Wicker Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wicker\_Man\_(2006\_film) "The Wicker Man (2006 film)")_, _[The Omen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Omen\_(2006\_film) "The Omen (2006 film)")_, _[Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween\_(2007\_film) "Halloween (2007 film)"),_ _[My Bloody Valentine 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Bloody\_Valentine\_3D "My Bloody Valentine 3D")_, _[Friday the 13th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday\_the\_13th\_(2009\_film) "Friday the 13th (2009 film)")_, _[A Nightmare on Elm Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Nightmare\_on\_Elm\_Street\_(2010\_film) "A Nightmare on Elm Street (2010 film)"),_ _[Carrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie\_(2013\_film) "Carrie (2013 film)"),_ and _[Poltergeist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poltergeist\_(2015\_film) "Poltergeist (2015 film)")_. These films were met with mixed to negative reviews and have been heavily criticized by audiences and critics alike for being unnecessary additions to their franchises.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Texas_Chainsaw_Massacre_(2003_film)#cite_note-51)
